fields.title: Prichal: three weeks to the conference, five weeks of work
fields.summary: The date was publicly announced two months ago. Decide what will be included in the launch.
fields.decisionPrompt: What will be included in the conference launch, and what will you say publicly?
fields.brief/role: You are the product manager for the team launching the invoicing module.
fields.brief/company: Prichal is a fictional company of 140 people that sells an operating system to logistics companies.
fields.brief/context: The module launches in three weeks at an industry conference: the date was publicly announced two months ago, and the CEO is giving a keynote there. This morning, development estimated the remaining work at five weeks against three weeks of capacity. Four items remain: multi-currency support, an invoice template editor, automatic payment reminders, and a data migration tool for existing clients.
fields.brief/objective: Launch at the conference with a usable product.
fields.brief/constraints: Three weeks, six developers, everyone is busy. The conference date cannot be moved. Anything missing at launch will be seen by clients and the press.
fields.brief/task: Decide what will be included in the launch and justify it.
fields.learnTakeaway/title: Scope is cut by the nature of the work, not by importance
fields.learnTakeaway/body: When the scope doesn't fit, the first step is to clarify what was actually promised—usually, it is much less than the team thinks. Next, look for cheap workarounds and identify what cannot be released half-done: half-baked financial features are worse than having none. And a stabilization buffer is not the last thing you cut; it is the one thing you never cut.
fields.evidenceCards/0/content:
Team capacity is 18 person-weeks over three weeks.

Multi-currency support: 6 weeks. Affects the pricing model, tax calculations, and the general ledger. Cannot be partially released: half-done currency support leads to incorrect invoices.

Invoice template editor: 7 weeks. Drag-and-drop blocks. Workaround: three ready-made templates that already work, costing zero effort.

Automatic payment reminders: 4 weeks. Workaround: a list of unpaid invoices and manual mailing, taking half a day of work.

Data migration for existing clients: 8 weeks. No workaround, but no urgency either: migration will happen after the launch.

Dev lead: "The estimates are honest; adding people at this stage won't help."
fields.evidenceCards/1/content:
There are 14 qualified deals in the module's pipeline.

Of those, 3 named multi-currency support as a requirement—these are the three largest deals.

0 mentioned the template editor.

2 asked about payment reminders.

There are 380 existing clients on the old billing system. All of the top 40 were surveyed: 6 want to transition in the first quarter after launch, the rest are indifferent or prefer to do it later.

Sales asks to "show at least something for templates": at the last conference, a competitor showed off their editor.
fields.evidenceCards/2/content:
The team worked two of the last four weekends. The dev lead raised burnout twice in one-on-one meetings.

There are 31 open defects in the already completed part of the module, including 4 critical ones: incorrect invoice amounts in certain cases of proportional calculation.

None of the 31 are in the current three-week plan.

QA lead's note: "Whatever you decide, I need five days of stabilization at the end, otherwise we will release something we'll be fixing for the entire next month."
fields.evidenceCards/3/content:
You reviewed public and contractual records.

The conference announcement says "billing rebuilt from scratch," without a feature list.

Two signed contracts have a clause about the module. Both explicitly name multi-currency support. Neither mentions the other three features. Delivery deadlines in both are a quarter after the conference, not the conference itself.

The draft of the CEO's keynote contains the phrase "billing for companies operating in multiple countries."

The press release is not yet approved: its text can be changed this week.
fields.decisionOptions/0/description: Release multi-currency support (6 weeks), fix critical defects, take five days for stabilization, provide ready-made templates, and handle reminders manually.
fields.decisionOptions/0/consequence:
The math works out: 6 weeks for currencies, about 4 weeks for critical defects and stabilization, leaving a buffer for the unexpected—against 18 person-weeks of capacity.
Multi-currency is the only feature named in the two contracts and the three largest deals, and the only one that cannot be released half-done.
There are no templates in the launch, but three ready-made ones cover the booth demo; not a single one of the 14 clients asked for the editor.
Reminders are handled via a list and manual mailing in half a day—the two clients who asked get a working process.
You rewrite the press release to focus on "billing for those operating in multiple countries"—the exact phrase from the CEO's keynote.
The launch goes smoothly without any incorrect amounts being exposed on stage.
Compromise: sales was left without a template editor for the competitor's conference, which was discussed twice.
fields.decisionOptions/1/description: Build what clients actually asked for: ten person-weeks against eighteen, leaving room for defects but not for full stabilization.
fields.decisionOptions/1/consequence:
Both features are released, and the launch looks richer.
However, ten weeks of work plus four critical defects leave no room for the five days of stabilization requested by QA.
A week after the conference, three of the 31 defects surface, two of them on new clients' invoices; a month is spent on fixes.
Meanwhile, manual mailing would have solved the problem for the two inquiring clients in half a day.
Compromise: real but non-urgent value was added at the expense of the quality buffer—the one part that should never be cut.
fields.decisionOptions/2/description: Release for both new and existing clients: fourteen person-weeks against eighteen, so the launch is not limited to new business.
fields.decisionOptions/2/consequence:
Fourteen weeks against eighteen looks doable right up until the first delay.
Data migration takes eight weeks, and it's work that cannot be rushed: it touches historical invoices.
The buffer for 31 defects and stabilization disappears; the team, having already worked two weekends, works a third.
Meanwhile, only 6 out of 40 surveyed clients want to transition in the first quarter: there is no urgency to justify this.
Compromise: work with a quarterly horizon was dragged into a three-week launch, and quality and people paid the price now.
fields.decisionOptions/3/description: Go to the CEO and propose releasing after the conference with the full scope, while showing a sneak peek during the keynote.
fields.decisionOptions/3/consequence:
The conversation happens, and it is not pointless: the CEO can indeed talk about the future rather than what is currently available.
However, the public announcement was made two months ago and did not include a feature list—meaning there is nothing to postpone: the promise was not a specific feature, but "billing rebuilt from scratch."
Meanwhile, multi-currency support fits the timeline, and two contracts explicitly name it.
The proposal looks like a request to cancel the date just because the editor doesn't fit—an editor that no one even asked for.
Compromise: the right question was considered—what was actually promised—but the answer was already available in the records and did not require a postponement.
fields.rubric/remediation/0/gap: Work order chosen by importance rather than cost of delay and size
fields.rubric/remediation/1/gap: Release is assembled from ready-made pieces and does not allow completing the task end-to-end
fields.rubric/remediation/2/gap: Risk is identified, but lacks a trigger, response plan, and owner
fields.rubric/remediation/3/gap: Undecided whose data is the source of truth and what happens if one side is unavailable
fields.rubric/remediation/4/gap: Transition is planned as a single switchover date without phases or rollback options
fields.rubric/remediation/5/gap: Training is reduced to instructions instead of on-the-job guidance
